extracted.intended_audience: biologists and statisticians performing empirical studies of correlation, regression, growth, and selection in populations
extracted.subtask_description: Procedures and quantitative criteria for measuring correlation and regression between characters (organs) in individuals and populations, for predicting one character from another, and for detecting selection from repeated samples. Emphasis on constructing correlation tables/arrays, computing means/standard deviations/correlation coefficients, and interpreting changes over time and with age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regression (phenomenon and interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: In associated or correlated pairs, if one member is selected with a given value for its character, the second has on average a less extreme value, 'regressing' toward the mean of the general population; if the selected member is below the mean the other regresses upward (progression).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by poppy capsule data: selecting capsules with 5, 6, 7, 13 bands shows the mode of the associated member shifts toward the population mode (10). Regression is visualised by the polygon of means (points a, b, c, d, ...) and by fitting a straight 'line of regression' through these mean points. If regression is zero the regression line is the 45° diagonal; if perfect regression (no correlation) the line is horizontal at the population mean.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation coefficient r (definition and interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The steepness (slope) of the regression line is termed the correlation and is represented by the letter r; r measures the degree of resemblance of like parts in the individual (or degree of association between two characters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for poppy capsules r = .56, which 'represents the degree of resemblance of like parts in the individual.' As r approaches unity prediction of one member from the other becomes more certain; correlation quantifies the transition from correlation to causation (higher r means B accompanies A in a larger proportion of cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation-table / array construction (arrays and frequencies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare a correlation table by selecting successively organs of a given size in one member of the pair and forming the array of the organs in the other member; the frequency under each column gives the distribution (array) of the associated organ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example arrays are given (e.g. array corresponding to 14: 4, 9, 27, 52, 35, 23, 28, 12). Columns and rows are added to form totals; the means and standard deviations of column totals and row totals give the types and variabilities of the two organs in the whole population. Arrays permit the plotting of the polygon of regression (means of arrays plotted vs selected value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended sample size for correlation studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure or count some character in pairs of organs of the same or different individuals for 500 to 1000 cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The method stages begin with measuring 500–1000 pairs to get reliable correlation tables and to form arrays with adequate frequencies for means and standard deviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute means and standard deviations of marginals (Mx, M2, σ1, σ2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Add up the columns and rows of the correlation table to form column and row totals; the means and standard deviations of these totals give the types and variabilities of the two organs in the whole population (denoted M1, M2 and σ1, σ2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These population marginals are the reference points for constructing regression lines and for later calculations (e.g. deviations x and y are measured from these means).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding regression lines and their slopes
rubrics_metrics.description: Find the means of each separate column array; the best-fitting straight line drawn through these means (when plotted) is the line of regression for the second organ on the first, and its slope = r·(σ2/σ1). The regression of the first on the second has slope r·(σ1/σ2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot column means against the selected values and fit the straight line minimising the sum of squared distances of the points from the line. The two regression lines (each regressing one organ on the other) intersect at the population means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formula for the correlation coefficient r (computational rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let x and y be deviations from their respective means for associated pairs; take the average value for all associated pairs of the product x·y and divide this by the product of the standard deviations σ1·σ2; the result is r, the correlation coefficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard moment-based definition: r = E[x y] / (σ1 σ2), where x = value_of_first - M1 and y = value_of_second - M2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regression equation for prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: The most probable value (mean of the array) of the second organ given a first organ value m1 = M1 + x is m2 = M2 + r·(σ2/σ1)·(m1 - M1). The coefficient r·(σ2/σ1) is termed the coefficient of regression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: the probable deviation of the second organ from its mean is the product of the coefficient of regression and the observed deviation of the first organ from its mean. When r = 0 there is no regression; when r = 1 regression is maximal (perfect correlation gives strongest prediction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction in variability from population to array (S^2 relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: If S is the standard deviation of an array about its regression-point and σ the standard deviation of the whole population, then the mean value of S^2 for all arrays is σ^2(1 − r^2); if regression is truly linear and certain hypotheses hold, the standard deviation of each array about its mean equals σ·√(1 − r^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus the coefficient of correlation determines the reduction in variability as we pass from the general population to a special array. High r (near unity) concentrates the distribution and makes prediction from one member to the other more precise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of growth of like parts (empirical regularity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of resemblance between undifferentiated like organs in the individual is nearly the same for all forms of life, and its mean value lies approximately in a fixed range (text states between about .4 and .5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pearson calls this the 'law of growth of like parts' — an empirical regularity suggesting that correlations of undifferentiated like parts are broadly similar across taxa; caveats: 'undifferentiated' must be emphasised (differentiated organs like fingers are not covered).

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for age when specifying types/variabilities/correlations
rubrics_metrics.description: State precisely the period of life (age) of individuals used; do not form numerical specification of a form of life by combining widely different ages because type, variability, and correlation change with age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: stature at 11 vs 13 years — means and variabilities change and the array-of-11-to-13 gives correlation measuring individuality of growth. For selection studies confine to stages with clearly marked adult condition unless age effects are explicitly modelled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting selection and decomposing death-rate (selective vs non-selective)
rubrics_metrics.description: To detect selection, measure types, variabilities, and correlations of the same organs at two epochs (samples of adults at two times). If they differ, the death-rate is partly selective; if not, it is non-selective. The total death-rate can be separated into selective and non-selective portions by comparing the two frequency polygons and scaling the later polygon inward until it just fits inside the earlier; the point of tangency corresponds to the character value with non-selective death-rate (best fitted to survive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical cautions: choose fair samples (e.g. two samples of 1000) and avoid migration or rapid environmental change. From differences in mode, mean, SD and skewness the mathematician can determine constants describing relative death-rates. Note limitation: while the scaling m can be found, n is unknown so absolute values or proportions of selective vs non-selective death-rates cannot always be obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure skewness by (mode − mean)/standard_deviation
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure skewness of a frequency distribution by the ratio of the distance between mode and mean to the standard deviation; the sign and magnitude describe asymmetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: two epoch illustration gives skewness .302 and −.303, showing selection can change type, variability, and even the sign of skewness. In practice determine modes more precisely than crude integer mode values used in illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical sampling and locality advice for temporal comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: When measuring change over time (selection) take reasonable precautions against migration and rapid environmental change in the locality; treat each epoch by fair samples (e.g. 1000 adults) as representative of the adult population at that time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This minimizes confounding due to immigration/emigration or transient environmental fluctuations that would bias perceived selection effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of correlation/regression for reconstruction and prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: Correlation and regression enable reconstruction of probable values of unobserved organs from measured organs (e.g. reconstruct stature from a set of long bones, or other parts from a single bone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerical values of correlation are now known for many human characters (table provided). Caveat: historical claims (e.g. Cuvier) were overstated in 1812; modern correlation allows probabilistic reconstruction but not complete certainty.
